claim: Preserved communication abilities promote healthy ageing.
source: Preserved communication abilities promote healthy ageing.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by established scientific understanding about healthy aging.

claim: The age-typical loss of sensory acuity might in part be compensated for by an individual's preserved attentional neural filtering.
source: To this end, the age-typical loss of sensory acuity might in part be compensated for by an individual's preserved attentional neural filtering.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential compensatory mechanism.

claim: Individual listening behaviour and neural filtering ability follow largely independent developmental trajectories in a cohort of N = 105 ageing individuals (39–82 y).
source: We here show that individual listening behaviour and neural filtering ability follow largely independent developmental trajectories modelling electroencephalographic and behavioural data of N = 105 ageing individuals (39–82 y).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Despite the expected decline in hearing-threshold-derived sensory acuity, listening-task performance proved stable over 2 y.
source: First, despite the expected decline in hearing-threshold-derived sensory acuity, listening-task performance proved stable over 2 y.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal data analysis.

claim: Neural filtering and behaviour were correlated only within each separate measurement timepoint (T1, T2).
source: Second, neural filtering and behaviour were correlated only within each separate measurement timepoint (T1, T2).
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-sectional analysis at each timepoint.

claim: Neither neural filtering at T1 nor its 2-year change could predict individual 2-year behavioural change.
source: Longitudinally, however, our results raise caution on attention-guided neural filtering metrics as predictors of individual trajectories in listening behaviour: neither neural filtering at T1 nor its 2-year change could predict individual 2-year behavioural change, under a combination of modelling strategies.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal change score modeling analysis.

claim: Speech comprehension is an essential aspect of human communication, enabling us to understand and interact with others effectively.
source: Speech comprehension is an essential aspect of human communication, enabling us to understand and interact with others effectively.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about human communication.

claim: Preserved communication is critical to social well-being and healthy ageing.
source: Preserved communication is therefore critical to social well-being and healthy ageing (Lindenberger, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: As we age, our ability to comprehend speech can decline due to age-related changes in the auditory system (i.e. sensory acuity) and in cognitive resources.
source: As we age, our ability to comprehend speech can decline due to age-related changes in the auditory system (i.e. sensory acuity) and in cognitive resources.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about aging and speech comprehension.

claim: Age-related hearing loss reduces the ability to detect and discriminate speech sounds, especially in noisy environments.
source: Age-related hearing loss reduces the ability to detect and discriminate speech sounds, especially in noisy environments.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about age-related hearing loss.

claim: Increasing age and hearing loss cannot fully account for the considerable degree of inter-individual differences observed in listening behaviour and its lifespan change.
source: However, it has long been recognised that increasing age and hearing loss cannot fully account for the considerable degree of inter-individual differences observed in listening behaviour and its lifespan change (Akeroyd, 2008; Houtgast and Festen, 2008; Humes et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural filter mechanisms act by selectively increasing the sensory gain for behaviourally relevant inputs or by inhibiting the processing of irrelevant inputs.
source: Such neural filter mechanisms act by selectively increasing the sensory gain for behaviourally relevant inputs or by inhibiting the processing of irrelevant inputs (Cherry, 1953; Broadbent, 1958; Wöstmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Speech comprehension is neurally supported by an attention-guided filter mechanism that modulates sensory gain and arises from primary auditory and perisylvian brain regions.
source: A growing body of evidence suggests that speech comprehension is neurally supported by an attention-guided filter mechanism that modulates sensory gain and arises from primary auditory and perisylvian brain regions: by synchronising its neural activity with the temporal structure of the speech signal of interest, the brain 'tracks' and thereby better encodes behaviourally relevant auditory inputs to enable attentive listening (Ding and Simon, 2012; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013; Obleser and Kayser, 2019; Lakatos et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In a large age-varying cohort (N = 155; 39–80 y), the fidelity of neural filtering strategy can help explain differences in listening behaviour from individual to individual and within individuals from sentence to sentence.
source: In a large age-varying cohort (N = 155; 39–80 y), we have previously shown how the fidelity of this neural filtering strategy can help explain differences in listening behaviour (i) from individual to individual and (ii) within individuals from sentence to sentence (Tune et al., 2021; O'Sullivan et al., 2015; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research including the authors' own previous work.

claim: Enhanced neural filtering—defined as stronger neural tracking of attended vs. ignored speech—led to more accurate and overall faster responses.
source: We observed that enhanced neural filtering—defined as stronger neural tracking of attended vs. ignored speech—led to more accurate and overall faster responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous research.

claim: Both neural filtering as well as its link to behaviour were independent of chronological age and severity of hearing loss.
source: Notably, we observed both neural filtering as well as its link to behaviour to be independent of chronological age and severity of hearing loss (Tune et al., 2021; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous research, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The longitudinal sample consisted of N = 105 individuals aged 39–82 y at T2 with a median age of 63 y.
source: We studied an age-varying cohort of healthy middle-aged and older adults longitudinally (N = 105, 39–82 y, median age at T2: 63 y).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The mean time difference between the two measurement timepoints was 23.2 (SD: 4.0) mo.
source: The mean time difference between the two measurement timepoints reported here was 23.2 (SD: 4.0) mo.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: Hearing acuity decreased linearly with increasing age (β = –3.4, standard error [SE] = 0.71, p<0.001).
source: As expected, hearing acuity decreased linearly with increasing age (Figure 3A, β = –3.4, standard error [SE] = 0.71, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the data, also shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Hearing acuity decreased on average by 1.2 dB from T1 to T2 (β = –1.18, SE = 0.27, p<0.001).
source: and on average by 1.2 dB from T1 to T2 (β = –1.18, SE = 0.27, p<0.001; meanT1: –13.72 dB HL [SD: 7.8]; meanT2: –14.90 dB HL [8.3]).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the longitudinal data.

claim: The effect of age on hearing acuity did not change with time (age × timepoint β = –0.35, SE = 0.28, p=0.21).
source: The effect of age did not change with time (age × timepoint β = –0.35, SE = 0.28, p=0.21).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis testing for interaction effects.

claim: The observed change in hearing acuity corresponds to a projected average decrease per decade of –6.3 (SD: 15.3) dB HL.
source: Assuming constant individual progression rates, this observed change corresponds to a projected average decrease in hearing acuity per decade of –6.3 (SD: 15.3) dB HL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data, also shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The magnitude of observed and projected hearing loss progression is well in line with recent large-sample reports.
source: The magnitude of observed and projected hearing loss progression is well in line with recent large-sample reports (Linssen et al., 2014; Rigters et al., 2018; Wiley et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to prior research cited.

claim: Measurements of hearing acuity showed high test–retest reliability (r = 0.94, p<0.001).
source: Measurements of hearing acuity showed high test–retest reliability (r = 0.94, p<0.001), underscoring the high fidelity of our audiological assessment.
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis of the hearing acuity measurements.

claim: Both behavioural outcomes (response speed and accuracy) declined with increasing age at T1 and T2 (speed: β = –0.02, SE = 0.01, p=0.004; accuracy: β = –0.23, SE = 0.07, p=0.0001).
source: In line with known deleterious effects of age, both behavioural outcomes (response speed and accuracy) declined with increasing age, and did so to a similar degree in T1 and T2 (Figure 3C and D; speed: β = –0.02, SE = 0.01, p=0.004; accuracy: β = –0.23, SE = 0.07, p=0.0001; timepoint × age p>0.12).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, also shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: Average performance levels remained stable from T1 to T2 (speed: β = 0.004, SE = 0.01, p=0.44; accuracy: β = 0.04, SE = 0.05, p=0.36).
source: At the same time and contrary to our expectations, average performance levels remained stable from T1 to T2 (speed: β = 0.004, SE = 0.01, p=0.44; meanT1: 0.62 s–1 [0.08]; meanT2: 0.62 s–1 [0.08]; accuracy: β = 0.04, SE = 0.05, p=0.36, meanT1: 0.88% [0.09]; meanT2: 0.88% [0.11]).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of longitudinal change in behavior.

claim: Accuracy and response speed showed moderately high test–retest reliability (speed: r = 0.70, p<0.001; accuracy: r = 0.72, p<0.001).
source: Accuracy and response speed showed moderately high test–retest reliability (speed: r = 0.70, p<0.001; accuracy: r = 0.72, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis of the behavioral measures.

claim: Neural filtering strength varied independently of age at both timepoints (β = 0.0003, SE = 0.0005, p=0.48; timepoint × age β = –0.0002, SE = 0.0006, p=0.79).
source: The analysis of change in neural filtering revealed that its strength varied independently of age at both timepoints (Figure 3B, β = 0.0003, SE = 0.0005, p=0.48; timepoint × age β = –0.0002, SE = 0.0006, p=0.79), confirming our previously reported T1 results (Tune et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, also shown in Figure 3B, and confirms prior results.

claim: There was no evidence of any systematic group-level change in neural filtering from T1 to T2 (β = 0.001, SE = 0.001, p=0.16).
source: As shown in Figure 3 (bottom-left panel), magnitude and direction of observed longitudinal change are highly variable across individuals and age groups, and we did not find evidence of any systematic group-level change from T1 to T2 (β = 0.001, SE = 0.001, p=0.16).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: Individual neural filtering strength correlated only weakly across time (r = 0.21, p=0.03).
source: In addition, individual neural filtering strength correlated only weakly across time (r = 0.21, p=0.03).
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis of the neural filtering measure.

claim: Individual alpha frequency (IAF) showed high test–retest reliability (r = 0.83, p<0.001).
source: As expected, both metrics showed high test–retest reliability (IAF: r = 0.83, p<0.001; 1/f slope: r = 0.78, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis of resting-state EEG metrics.

claim: The slope of 1/f neural noise showed high test–retest reliability (r = 0.78, p<0.001).
source: As expected, both metrics showed high test–retest reliability (IAF: r = 0.83, p<0.001; 1/f slope: r = 0.78, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the reliability analysis of resting-state EEG metrics.

claim: Higher age was associated with poorer hearing ability (β = –0.43, SE = 0.09, p<0.001).
source: Our expectations on the direct relationships were indeed borne out by the data: higher age was associated with poorer hearing ability (β = –0.43, SE = 0.09, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the causal mediation analysis.

claim: Higher age was associated with poorer listening performance (speed: β = –0.33, SE = 0.06, p<0.001; accuracy: β = –0.26, SE = 0.06, p<0.001).
source: and listening performance (speed: β = –0.33, SE = 0.06, p<0.001; accuracy: β = –0.26, SE = 0.06, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the causal mediation analysis.

claim: Better hearing ability boosted accuracy but not response speed (accuracy: β = 0.30, SE = 0.1, p=0.003; speed: β = –0.06, SE = 0.1, p=0.56).
source: Better hearing ability, on the other hand, boosted accuracy but not response speed (accuracy: β = 0.30, SE = 0.1, p=0.003; speed: β = –0.06, SE = 0.1, p=0.56).
evidence: This is a finding from the causal mediation analysis.

claim: The direct effects of age and hearing on behavior remained stable from T1 to T2 (all interactions by timepoint p>0.56; all log Bayes factors [logBF01] >2.5).
source: These direct effects remained stable from T1 to T2 (all interactions by timepoint p>0.56; all log Bayes factors [logBF01] >2.5).
evidence: This is a finding from the moderated mediation analysis.

claim: The total effect of age on accuracy was partially mediated via its detrimental effect on hearing acuity (average causal mediation effect [ACME], β = –0.12, SE = 0.04, p<0.001).
source: Age also impacted accuracy indirectly: the total effect of age was partially mediated via its detrimental effect on hearing acuity (average causal mediation effect [ACME], β = –0.12, SE = 0.04, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the causal mediation analysis.

claim: There was no evidence for an indirect effect of age on speed mediated by hearing acuity (ACME: β = 0.008, SE = 0.03, p=0.77).
source: We did not find evidence for an analogous indirect effect on speed (ACME: β = 0.008, SE = 0.03, p=0.77).
evidence: This is a finding from the causal mediation analysis.

claim: The hearing-acuity-mediated effect of age on accuracy did not change from T1 to T2 (interaction by timepoint p=0.73).
source: Again, the hearing-acuity-mediated effect of age on accuracy did not change from T1 to T2 as evidenced by moderated mediation analysis (interaction by timepoint p=0.73).
evidence: This is a finding from the moderated mediation analysis.

claim: Stronger neural filtering fidelity had a beneficial effect on both measures of listening performance (accuracy: β = 0.21, SE = 0.09, p=0.02; speed: β = 0.33, SE = 0.09, p<0.001).
source: Speaking to the robustness of our previous results, we observed the beneficial effect of stronger neural filtering fidelity on both measures of listening performance (accuracy: β = 0.21, SE = 0.09, p=0.02; speed: β = 0.33, SE = 0.09, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the causal mediation analysis.

claim: The longitudinal stability of the direct brain–behaviour link was supported by the absence of any significant changes with time (interactions by timepoint; all p>0.28, all logBF01 > 2.1).
source: Most importantly, the longitudinal stability of the observed direct brain–behaviour link was further supported by the absence of any significant changes with time (interactions by timepoint; all p>0.28, all logBF01 > 2.1).
evidence: This is a finding from the moderated mediation analysis.

claim: Stronger single-trial neural filtering was associated with higher listening success at both T1 and T2 (odds ratio [OR] = 1.08, SE = 0.02, p<0.001; interaction neural filtering × timepoint: OR = 0.99, SE = 0.03, p=0.82).
source: Lending credibility to our previous results, stronger single-trial neural filtering was associated with higher listening success at both T1 and T2 (logistic mixed-effect model; within-participant effect of neural filtering on accuracy: odds ratio [OR] = 1.08, SE = 0.02, p<0.001; interaction neural filtering × timepoint: OR = 0.99, SE = 0.03, p=0.82; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the single-trial mixed-effect model analysis, also shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Listening task accuracy remained stable on average (b0 = 0.053, SE = 0.045, Δχ2(df = 1) = 1.33, p=0.25).
source: On average, listening task accuracy remained stable (b0 = 0.053, SE = 0.045, Δχ2(df = 1) = 1.33, p=0.25).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariate latent change score model.

claim: Response speed showed a significant mean increase over time (b0 = 0.13, SE = 0.03, Δχ2(df = 1) = 12.79, p<0.001).
source: Response speed, on the other hand, showed a significant mean increase over time (b0 = 0.13, SE = 0.03, Δχ2(df = 1) = 12.79, p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariate latent change score model, also shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The model of neural filtering showed a (marginally) significant mean increase (b0 = 0.24, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.98, p=0.08).
source: Similarly, the model of neural filtering showed a (marginally) significant mean increase (b0 = 0.24, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.98, p=0.08; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the univariate latent change score model, also shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was reliable variance (i.e. individual differences) in the longitudinal change in both speed (standardised estimate ϕ = 0.88, SE = 0.07, Δχ2(df = 5) = 94.07, p<0.01) and neural filtering (ϕ = 0.81, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 4) = 25.64, p<.001).
source: Crucial to our change-related inquiries, we observed reliable variance (i.e. individual differences) in the longitudinal change in both speed (standardised estimate ϕ = 0.88, SE = 0.07, Δχ2(df = 5) = 94.07, p<0.01) and neural filtering (ϕ = 0.81, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 4) = 25.64, p<.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: Individuals with relatively strong neural filtering or fast responses at T1 showed a smaller increase from T1 to T2 (speed: β = –0.43, SE = 0.12, Δχ2(df = 1) = 8.75, p=0.003; neural filtering: β = –0.44, SE = 0.16, Δχ2(df = 1) = 4.17, p=0.04).
source: Individuals' baseline levels of both speed and neural filtering strength were predictive of their respective longitudinal change: individuals with relatively strong neural filtering or fast responses at T1 showed a smaller increase from T1 to T2, possibly indicating ceiling effects (speed: β = –0.43, SE = 0.12, Δχ2(df = 1) = 8.75, p=0.003; neural filtering: β = –0.44, SE = 0.16, Δχ2(df = 1) = 4.17, p=0.04).
evidence: This is a finding from the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: The older a participant at T1, the smaller their longitudinal increase in speed (speed: ϕ = –0.24, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 4.38, p=0.037).
source: We also observed that participants' age at T1 covaried with the individual degree of change in speed but not with that in neural filtering: The older a participant at T1, the smaller their longitudinal increase in speed (speed: ϕ = –0.24, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 4.38, p=0.037; neural filtering: ϕ = –0.02, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.02, p=0.89).
evidence: This is a finding from the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: Age at T1 did not covary with the individual degree of change in neural filtering (neural filtering: ϕ = –0.02, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.02, p=0.89).
source: We also observed that participants' age at T1 covaried with the individual degree of change in speed but not with that in neural filtering: The older a participant at T1, the smaller their longitudinal increase in speed (speed: ϕ = –0.24, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 4.38, p=0.037; neural filtering: ϕ = –0.02, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.02, p=0.89).
evidence: This is a finding from the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: An individual's latent T1 level of neural filtering strength was not predictive of the ensuing latent T1–T2 change in response speed (β = 0.02, SE = 0.16, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.02, p=0.90).
source: Importantly, however, an individual's latent T1 level of neural filtering strength was not predictive of the ensuing latent T1–T2 change in response speed (β = 0.02, SE = 0.16, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.02, p=0.90).
evidence: This is a finding from the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: An individual's latent T1 level of response speed was not predictive of the ensuing latent T1–T2 change in neural filtering (β = –0.11, SE = 0.21, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.31, p=0.58).
source: Still, in a control analysis that freely estimated the respective path, we found that an individual's latent T1 level of response speed was not predictive of the ensuing latent T1–T2 change in neural filtering (β = –0.11, SE = 0.21, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.31, p=0.58).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis of the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: Longitudinal change in the neural and the behavioural domain occurred largely independent of one another (ϕ = 0.25, SE = 0.15, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.74, p=0.1).
source: Change score modelling revealed that longitudinal change in the neural and the behavioural domain occurred largely independent of one another despite their systematic relationship within each separate measurement timepoint (ϕ = 0.25, SE = 0.15, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.74, p=0.1).
evidence: This is a finding from the bivariate latent change score model.

claim: Linking response speed and neural filtering under selective attention strengthened their relationship at T1 (ϕ = 0.54, SE = 0.15, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.74, p=0.1).
source: As shown in Figure 6, taken together, the control analyses provide compelling empirical support for the robustness of our main results: linking response speed and neural filtering under selective attention strengthened their relationship at T1 (ϕ = 0.54, SE = 0.15, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.74, p=0.1; Figure 6B; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis, also shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the control analysis with selective attention trials, T1 neural filtering did not predict behavioural change (β = 0.13, SE = 0.21, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.43, p=0.51).
source: but did not yield any significant effects for the influence of T1 neural filtering on behavioural change (β = 0.13, SE = 0.21, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.43, p=0.51),
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis.

claim: In the control analysis with selective attention trials, the relationship of neural and behavioural change was not significant (ϕ = 0.26, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 1) = 3.1, p=0.08).
source: or for the relationship of neural and behavioural change (ϕ = 0.26, SE = 0.14, Δχ2(df = 1) = 3.1, p=0.08; please note the close correspondence to path estimates reported in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis.

claim: Neural tracking of attended speech showed substantially higher manifest-level test–retest reliability (r = 0.65, p<0.001) compared to that of the neural tracking index.
source: The second control analysis revealed a substantially higher manifest-level test–retest reliability of neural tracking of attended speech (r = 0.65, p<0.001; Figure 6C, see also Figure 6—figure supplement 2 for neural tracking of ignored speech) compared to that of the neural tracking index.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis, also shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the control analysis with attended-speech tracking, baseline levels of attended-speech tracking did not predict future change in response speed (β = 0.18, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.73, p=0.10).
source: However, when linked to longitudinal changes in response speed, this analysis provided even less evidence for systematic change-related relationships: baseline levels of attended-speech tracking did not predict future change in response speed (β = 0.18, SE = 0.11, Δχ2(df = 1) = 2.73, p=0.10),
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis.

claim: In the control analysis with attended-speech tracking, changes in neural and behavioural functioning occurred independently of one another (ϕ = –0.03, SE = 0.12, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.06, p=0.81).
source: and changes in neural and behavioural functioning occurred independently of one another (ϕ = –0.03, SE = 0.12, Δχ2(df = 1) = 0.06, p=0.81).
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis.

claim: Dropout at T2 could not be predicted from participants' T1 age, hearing loss, behavioural performance (accuracy, speed), or neural filtering strength (all p>0.13).
source: Dropout at T2 could not be predicted from participants' T1 age, hearing loss, behavioural performance (accuracy, speed), or neural filtering strength (all p>0.13).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of dropout patterns.

claim: The reduced longitudinal sample was not biased in terms of sensory, cognitive, or neural functioning compared to the full T1 cohort.
source: This indicates that compared to the full T1 cohort reported on in previous studies (Tune et al., 2021; Alavash et al., 2021) our reduced longitudinal sample was not biased in terms of sensory, cognitive, or neural functioning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dropout analysis.

claim: Participants gave written informed consent and received financial compensation (10€ per hour).
source: Participants gave written informed consent and received financial compensation (10€ per hour).
evidence: This is a description of the study procedures.

claim: Procedures were approved by the ethics committee of the University of Lübeck and were in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: Procedures were approved by the ethics committee of the University of Lübeck and were in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
